title: Trump Orders H-1B Approvals to Weigh Employer Layoffs, Extends $100,000 Fee
excerpt: The September 18 executive order directs five federal agencies to scrutinize layoffs when adjudicating H-1B petitions and orders a 30-day review of previously filed labor applications, while a companion proclamation extends the $100,000 fee through September 2027.
body:
• On September 18, President Trump signed an executive order requiring federal agencies to consider an employer's recent or planned layoffs of U.S. workers when adjudicating H-1B petitions, labor condition applications, visas, and entries.
  • Five agencies must now coordinate on H-1B decisions — State, Labor, and Homeland Security, joined by Commerce, Education, and the Small Business Administration — and the Labor Department will review previously filed labor applications within 30 days.
  • A same-day proclamation extends the $100,000 H-1B payment requirement for covered cases involving workers outside the United States through September 21, 2027.
  • Both measures land hardest on Indian professionals, the largest group of H-1B beneficiaries, even as a federal judge's June ruling that blocked the fee is reviewed by a Boston appeals court.

President Donald Trump signed an executive order on September 18, 2026, directing federal agencies to scrutinize employers' layoff records when deciding H-1B cases, the most consequential tightening of the skilled-worker visa program in years. The order, titled "Enhancing Program Integrity and Interagency Coordination in the Administration of the H-1B Nonimmigrant Visa Program," was announced alongside a proclamation extending the administration's controversial $100,000 H-1B fee through September 21, 2027.

The layoffs provision is the sharper of the two moves. Section 3(a) of the order directs agencies to consider whether an H-1B sponsor conducted layoffs within the previous year, or plans future layoffs, that negatively affect similarly situated American workers — and to weigh those facts when adjudicating labor condition applications, H-1B petitions, visas, and entries into the United States, according to the Erickson Immigration Group's analysis of the order.

What the order changes

The order formalizes coordination among agencies that have historically handled H-1B decisions in parallel: the Departments of State, Labor, and Homeland Security must now work with the Departments of Commerce and Education and the Small Business Administration, which will supply wage, employment, academic, industrial, and economic information relevant to H-1B adjudications. The administration's framing is that no single agency has a complete picture of whether a foreign hire displaces American workers.

Separately, the order instructs the Labor Department's Wage and Hour Division to begin reviewing already-submitted labor condition applications within 30 days to assess whether enforcement action is warranted — a retrospective review that could expose sponsors to investigations over wages, worksite postings, benching, displacement, or the accuracy of information supplied in their filings. Immigration attorney Cyrus Mehta notes that the directive cannot retroactively turn a lawful filing into a violation merely because the employer later reduced its workforce, since a labor condition application is largely an attestation-based filing and the department's authority to reject or investigate it remains bounded by statute.

The $100,000 fee, extended

The companion proclamation, "Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers," extends for 12 months the $100,000 payment requirement first imposed in September 2025 for covered H-1B cases involving workers outside the United States, with a national-interest exception. The fee does not apply to all applicants: foreign nationals already in the U.S. on student visas who move to H-1B status are exempt, as are existing H-1B holders renewing their visas — a significant carve-out, since students converting to H-1B represent a large share of new recipients, according to the Asian Mirror's reporting.

The fee's legal footing remains uncertain. A federal judge ruled in June that the higher fee was illegal and blocked the administration from collecting it; the case is now under review by a Boston-based appeals court. A separate challenge brought by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the country's largest business lobbying group, is also working its way through the courts after a lower court rejected the group's case.

Why this matters for Indian professionals

Indians remain by far the largest beneficiaries of the H-1B program, which means every tightening — the layoffs scrutiny, the interagency data-sharing, the extended fee — falls disproportionately on Indian tech workers and the consulting and staffing firms that sponsor them. The White House has pointed to a 92% drop in registrations from large IT staffing and outsourcing firms as evidence the policy is working as intended, while critics in the diaspora argue the measures punish legal, high-skilled migration without fixing the underlying quota system.

Employers that have conducted or are planning reductions in force involving roles similar to sponsored H-1B positions will now need to address those circumstances directly in their filing records, a new compliance burden that immigration lawyers say favors large companies with sophisticated counsel and raises the barrier for smaller sponsors.

What's next

The order authorizes implementing rules, policies, and operational guidance to fold layoff and labor-market information into H-1B administration consistent with existing law — meaning the real impact will depend on how aggressively agencies write the follow-on rules. Immigration attorneys expect lawsuits challenging the layoffs directive, similar to those already targeting the fee, and the Labor Department's 30-day review of past labor applications is the first concrete deadline to watch. For H-1B workers and sponsors, the September 2027 fee horizon and the new layoffs lens make the next year of filings the most scrutinized in the program's history.
